A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SOLAR for predicting individual redditors' moral judgments through value abstraction and retrieval. All 13 pages of v1 and 16 pages of v2, including appendices, were readable. The substantial revisions support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original prediction experiments in Tables 2–3 and analyses of redditors' value preferences in Figures 2–3.

after.justification: V2 reports original 100-redditor evaluations, retrieval and input comparisons, and additional data-distribution, value-mapping and performance analyses in the appendices.

M1.justification: V1's selected SOLAR variant uses value-trade-off retrieval. V2 Section 5.2 introduces conditional retrieval: value-based retrieval for situations with below 70% judgment agreement and situation-based retrieval otherwise, using comments plus value trade-offs in prompts. This adds a substantive test-time selection procedure to the retained abstraction framework.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from eight exceptionally active redditors to 100, including substantially less-active users, with explicit evaluations of users with limited histories. This broadens the represented population beyond merely increasing samples. The subreddit, collection period and binary acceptability task remain the same.

E2.justification: V2 removes the random-author, random-comment, title-plus-judgment and differing-judgment comparisons. V1's hierarchical generator-plus-DeBERTa comparisons also disappear; v2 distinguishes direct encoder-decoder classification from comment/judgment generation. Its Table 3 introduces explicit comparisons combining different retrieval representations and prompt contents.

E3.justification: V2 changes judgment inference from GPT-4o to GPT-4.1 and reports text-embedding-3-large instead of text-embedding-3-small for value clustering. It revises the stated fine-tuning batch sizes and learning rates and introduces fivefold evaluation. The 60/10/30 split proportions and five retrieved examples remain.

E4.justification: V2 adds retrieval-versus-prompt-value ablations, retrieval distance versus history size, dataset representativeness checks, mappings between generated and Schwartz values, and performance analyses by history size and judgment balance. V1's Section 6.4 and Figure 3 analysis relating value distances to preference correlations is removed, rather than relocated.

E5.justification: V1's benchmark tables report point estimates. V2 first documents fivefold baseline evaluation and two LLM prompting runs to estimate confidence intervals, adding uncertainty terms throughout Tables 2–3. The confidence level and interval construction remain unspecified. These disclosures do not establish how many runs were performed for v1.

E6.justification: The principal results are extensively replaced and expanded. V1 reports SOLAR at 78.06 overall and 60.63 on controversial cases; v2 reports 79.90 and 82.44, alongside new 100-user and history-stratified results. These involve different populations, inference models and retrieval procedures, so they are not same-setting gains. Several top-eight baseline means remain numerically unchanged.

T1.justification: V2 adds notation for users, histories and embeddings and expresses retrieval in Equations 1–2. These formalize the nearest-neighbor procedures already described in v1, without introducing a new mathematical result, derivation or formal property. Neither version supplies theoretical proofs.

C1.justification: The central contributions—individual-level subjectivity modeling through value trade-offs, improved judgment prediction and explanatory value preferences—remain. V2 adds an explicit claim of particular benefit for users with limited data in its abstract, introduction and conclusion, extending v1's emphasis on overall and controversial-case performance.

C2.justification: V2 develops an explanation linking sparse histories, less topically similar retrieval and the usefulness of abstract values. It also interprets generated values as combining multiple Schwartz dimensions. V1's claim that the correlation analysis validates consistent preferences is removed, while v2 explicitly acknowledges possible value changes over time.

D1.justification: V2 supplies a code/data repository link, annotation and inference prompt templates, a specific annotation-model version and exact baseline checkpoint names. It replaces the generic tuning recipe with model-specific settings and revises hardware, timing and API-cost information, including batch pricing. V1's LoRA hyperparameter disclosure is removed.

R1.justification: Section 7 adds substantial positioning against research on values and LLMs, including Van Der Meer, Bhatia, Sorensen and Ye, and adds Plepi's work on personalized social-norm judgments. It explicitly distinguishes actual-user analysis, finer value categories and trade-off explanations. Earlier citations, including Li 2018 and Santurkar 2023, are removed.

P1.justification: V2 substantially rewrites the retained method, prompting, baseline and discussion passages. It consolidates controversial-case discussion into Section 6.1, reorganizes the appendices, and changes 'Subjectivity Abstraction' to 'Value Abstraction.' The title adds SOLAR, and an acknowledgements section is added.

P2.justification: Tables 2–3 are redesigned into separate baseline and RAG comparisons with grouped user columns. The value heatmap is transposed and directly labeled; several analytical plots and colored prompt boxes are added, while the consistency plot is removed. The overview diagram and UMAP visualization are retained, with the latter renumbered.

improvement.justification: The broader user coverage, targeted retrieval/input ablations and fuller prompt and access information improve on v1's narrow eight-user study. However, v2 removes randomized controls useful for assessing personalization and leaves unclear how its ensemble obtains test-situation agreement without relying on judgments being predicted. Its 1.7K situation count in Section 3.1 and Appendix A also conflicts with Table 1's 17,432. These shortcomings limit the net gain in empirical validation despite useful improvements in coverage and documentation.
